questions.scenario: An HR generalist must update a 40-page employee handbook so it reflects a 6-page legal memo describing new leave rules. Last time she pasted both documents and asked for the updated handbook in one go. The result rewrote a section the memo never mentions and missed one of the rule changes.
questions.stem: She is now redoing the job as a series of steps. Where should she put her most important review checkpoint so errors are caught before they spread, with the least extra effort?

options.text: After Claude has rewritten the whole handbook, by reading all 40 pages line by line before it is published.
Before the first step, by asking Claude to confirm it understands the memo and will be careful with every change.
After Claude lists each rule change in the memo and the handbook sections it affects, before any rewriting starts.
After each handbook section is rewritten, by asking Claude to rate its own confidence that the section is accurate.

questions.explanation: Both failures (an untouched section rewritten, a rule change missed) come from the first stage: working out **what changes where**. If Claude first produces a short list of rule changes mapped to handbook sections, she can check it against the memo in a few minutes. Every later step then builds on a verified change list. This is the point of splitting work into chained steps: each step's output can be inspected before anything is built on it, so the check belongs where an early error would otherwise flow into everything after it. A final read before publishing is still sensible, but it is not the checkpoint that stops the error spreading.

whyWrong.A: A final read is useful, but it is the most expensive place to catch a problem: the error has already been built into 40 pages, and a missing change is hard to notice when you are reading finished prose.
whyWrong.B: Asking Claude to promise care adds emphasis, not information. It gives her nothing to check and does not change how the work is structured.
whyWrong.D: A model's self-rated confidence is not a reliable accuracy signal, and a per-section check happens after the change list (where the errors start) has already been used.

questions.mindset: Put the human check at the step whose errors would flow into everything downstream.

questions.stem: A sales coordinator wants Claude to turn three bullet points into a short, friendly reminder email to a client about tomorrow's meeting. A colleague tells her to always split work into gather, outline, draft and review steps. What is the BEST approach for this request?

options.text: Write one clear prompt with the bullet points, the audience and the tone, then read the draft quickly before sending.
Ask for an outline of the email first, approve it, then request the draft, and finally ask Claude to critique it.
Have Claude list the facts from the bullet points in one turn, then draft the email from that list in a second turn.
Draft the email in one turn, then open a new chat and have Claude review the draft against a detailed checklist.

questions.explanation: Decomposition costs extra turns and extra time. It pays off when a task has distinct stages, produces something long or high-stakes, or needs a decision partway through. A three-point reminder email has none of these. One well-specified prompt (facts, audience, tone) plus a quick human read is the proportionate approach. Anthropic's guidance frames chaining as worth it when you need to inspect intermediate outputs, which this task does not.

whyWrong.B: Four steps for a short reminder adds time without adding quality. There is no outline worth approving in a few sentences.
whyWrong.C: The facts are already in her bullet points. Restating them in a separate turn adds a step with nothing to check.
whyWrong.D: A fresh-chat checklist review is over-engineering for a low-stakes, short email. Her own quick read covers the risk.

questions.mindset: Decompose when the task has stages or stakes; a short, simple request needs one good prompt.

questions.scenario: A customer-experience lead exports about 300 free-text comments from a weekly satisfaction survey (personal details already removed). She asks Claude to "categorize these and tell me the top issues." When she ran the same request on the next week's comments, Claude produced a different set of category names, so the two weeks cannot be compared.
questions.stem: Which way of restructuring the work would MOST reliably give her results she can compare week to week?

options.text: Ask Claude to use more specific category names and to stay consistent with whatever categories it chose last week.
Paste both weeks of comments into one prompt every time so Claude always categorizes them together.
Switch to the most capable model available so its judgment about categories is more stable over time.
First have Claude propose categories from a sample, approve and save that list, then classify each week against it.

questions.explanation: The inconsistency comes from Claude inventing the category scheme fresh every time. Splitting the job into two stages fixes the cause: **define the taxonomy once** (Claude proposes from a sample, she edits and approves), then **classify each week against that fixed list**. Saving the list in a Project's instructions or knowledge keeps it available for every week's chat. Providing a fixed structure and chaining steps are documented ways to make output consistent.

whyWrong.A: "Stay consistent with last week" relies on Claude knowing last week's categories, which a new chat does not. Asking for more specific names does not fix the scheme drifting.
whyWrong.B: Re-categorizing an ever-growing pile each week is slow, gets worse over time, and still lets the category names change between runs.
whyWrong.C: A bigger model is a heavy fix for a structure problem. Without a fixed category list, any model can name categories differently from run to run.

questions.mindset: When results must be comparable over time, fix the framework in its own step and reuse it.

questions.scenario: A finance operations analyst has a three-turn routine in Claude. Turn 1 extracts invoice totals from pasted vendor statements. Turn 2 calculates each department's variance against budget. Turn 3 writes a variance commentary for department heads. She copies each output straight into the next turn. A department head noticed a wrong figure in the commentary; it had been misread from a statement in turn 1.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes to her routine would MOST effectively stop this kind of error reaching department heads? Choose TWO.

options.text: Merge the three turns back into one prompt so Claude can cross-check the numbers across all steps at once.
Check the totals extracted in turn 1 against the source statements before they are used in the variance step.
Add the instruction "double-check every number carefully" to the turn 3 prompt that writes the commentary.
Add a fourth turn where Claude confirms that the figures in the commentary match the totals from turn 1.
Have turn 1 list, next to each total, the statement and line it came from, so she can spot-check quickly.

questions.explanation: She already decomposed the task, but she skipped the point of decomposing: **checking intermediate output**. The error started in extraction, so the check belongs right after turn 1 (B). Asking turn 1 to show where each total came from (E) makes that check fast and practical, because she can go straight to the source line. Together they create a real checkpoint at the step where errors begin, before they spread into the variance figures and the commentary.

whyWrong.A: Going back to one big prompt removes the intermediate output she needs to inspect. It makes the error harder to find, not easier.
whyWrong.C: Emphasis added at the last step does nothing about a figure that was misread two steps earlier. The commentary step never sees the source statements.
whyWrong.D: This check compares the commentary with the turn 1 totals, which are the wrong numbers. It would pass. It checks consistency, not correctness against the source.

questions.mindset: Decomposition only helps if someone checks the intermediate output against the real source.

questions.scenario: A program manager is writing a 12-section annual report for a funder with Claude. She approved an outline, then had Claude draft the sections one at a time. Sections 1 to 6 are good, but section 7 describes the project's evaluation method incorrectly.

options.text: Give Claude the correct details of the evaluation method and ask it to redraft only section 7 against the approved outline.
Restart from the outline step so every section is regenerated with the correct evaluation method in mind.
Regenerate section 7 several times and keep whichever version describes the evaluation method most accurately.
Carry on drafting sections 8 to 12 and fix the description of the method in one final editing pass at the end.

questions.explanation: One of the main benefits of working in steps is that **you can fix one step without redoing everything**. The outline and sections 1 to 6 are approved, so only section 7 needs work. The mistake is factual, so Claude needs the missing information (the correct method), not another roll of the dice. Fixing it now also stops later sections, such as results that depend on the method, from building on the error.

whyWrong.B: Regenerating approved work throws away good sections and creates new ones to re-check, all to fix one section.
whyWrong.C: Regenerating without giving the correct facts just produces different guesses. Claude does not know the real method unless she tells it.
whyWrong.D: Later sections, such as the results and lessons learned, may describe or depend on the evaluation method, so the error could spread before the final pass.

questions.mindset: Fix the faulty step with the missing information, and keep the steps you already approved.

questions.stem: An office manager asks Claude, in one prompt, to "compare these five venue brochures and pick the best one for our 150-person offsite." Claude picks an attractive venue that is 90 minutes from the office and over budget. Distance and budget matter a lot to her, but she never mentioned them. Which way of splitting the task would MOST improve the next attempt?

options.text: Ask Claude to compare the five brochures again and to explain its reasoning in much more detail before it chooses.
Ask Claude to shortlist its top three venues instead of a single one so that she has more options to choose from.
First agree the decision criteria and their priority (budget, travel time, capacity), then score each venue.
Have Claude summarize each brochure on its own first, then ask it to pick the venue it thinks fits best overall.

questions.explanation: The recommendation went wrong because the **criteria were never set**, so Claude used its own idea of "best". The right first step is to agree the criteria and their priority. Only then should Claude score each option against them and recommend one. This puts her judgment at the stage that controls everything after it, and the final choice becomes traceable ("Venue B wins on budget and travel time").

whyWrong.A: More detailed reasoning is still reasoning toward the wrong goal. Without her criteria, Claude would explain the same mistaken choice at greater length.
whyWrong.B: A shortlist chosen without her criteria may still leave out the venues that fit her budget and distance needs. It spreads the guess around without fixing it.
whyWrong.D: Summarizing each brochure is a reasonable split, but the final "best overall" step still has no criteria, so the same mistake can happen.

questions.mindset: Agree how the decision will be judged before asking Claude to make it.

questions.scenario: A policy officer spends a long conversation with Claude. She pastes three consultation responses, asks for the key themes, corrects two themes Claude got wrong, and moves on to other questions. About thirty turns later she asks Claude to draft a briefing note "based on the themes," and the draft uses one of the original, uncorrected themes.
questions.stem: Which approach would MOST reliably prevent this when she moves from the analysis step to the drafting step?

options.text: Tell Claude at the start of the conversation to always remember her corrections and apply them to everything it writes later.
Regenerate the briefing note until a version appears that uses the corrected themes instead of the original ones.
Write "use the themes we agreed on earlier" in the drafting prompt so Claude knows which version to follow.
Paste the corrected, approved list of themes into the drafting prompt and ask Claude to base the note only on that list.

questions.explanation: In a long conversation, the original and corrected themes are both in the context, and "the themes" is ambiguous. The reliable handoff between steps is to **pass the verified output of one step explicitly into the next**: paste the approved list and say the note must be based only on it. This is how chained steps are meant to connect. Each step gets a clear, checked input instead of relying on the model to work out which earlier version counts.

whyWrong.A: A general instruction to remember corrections is vague. Thirty turns later, both versions are still in the conversation and the same ambiguity remains.
whyWrong.B: Regenerating without changing the input leaves the outcome to chance. She still has to check every version, and nothing stops a repeat.
whyWrong.C: "Agreed earlier" still makes Claude search a long history for the right version, which is the same ambiguity that caused the problem. An explicit list removes it.

questions.mindset: Hand each step a clean, verified input; don't make the next step dig it out of history.

questions.stem: Which TWO features of a request are the strongest signs that it should be split into separate steps with review points, rather than handled in a single prompt? Choose TWO.

options.text: Later analysis depends on facts that must be correct before anything is built on them.
The request is urgent and the person wants an answer as fast as possible.
The request uses specialized vocabulary from the person's own industry.
A person needs to make a decision partway through, such as choosing an option.
The person plans to use the most capable model available for the task.

questions.explanation: Chaining exists so you can **inspect and branch on intermediate outputs**. That matters most in two situations: when **errors at one stage would spread to later stages** (A), because a checkpoint catches them early, and when **a human decision is needed midway** (D), because the work can pause for that decision instead of Claude guessing. Extra steps cost time, so they should be spent where a check or a decision adds the most protection.

whyWrong.B: Urgency argues against extra steps, since chaining trades speed for the ability to check intermediate results. Being urgent does not mean a task has stages to split.
whyWrong.C: Specialized vocabulary is handled by giving context or definitions in the prompt. It does not mean the task has separate stages.
whyWrong.E: Model choice does not decide whether a task has separate stages. A capable model still benefits from checkpoints on a multi-stage task, and a simple task needs none.

questions.mindset: Split work where errors would spread or where a human must decide.

questions.stem: A communications specialist is writing a public FAQ about a change to a council service. The answers must meet her organization's plain-language standard: short sentences, no jargon, and a set reading level. Her prompt asks Claude to write the FAQ and "make sure it follows the attached standard," but several answers still contain jargon. What is the MOST effective change to how she structures the work?

options.text: Repeat the standard in capital letters at the top and the bottom of the prompt so Claude gives it more weight.
After drafting, add a separate step where Claude checks each answer against the standard and lists every breach for her to review.
Add several more example FAQ answers to the prompt so Claude can copy the style of finished, compliant answers.
Switch to the most capable model so it can apply the plain-language standard while writing, without extra steps.

questions.explanation: Writing and checking against a detailed standard are two different jobs. When one prompt does both, the check gets less attention. Anthropic's canonical chaining pattern is **self-correction as separate steps**: draft, then review against explicit criteria, then refine. A dedicated review step produces a list of breaches she can see and confirm, so she knows what is being fixed and can catch anything the review missed.

whyWrong.A: Capital letters add emphasis but no new information, and the writing step still has to juggle drafting and compliance at once.
whyWrong.C: Examples help with style, but they do not systematically check each answer against every rule. Jargon can still get through without anyone noticing.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model is a heavy fix and still leaves no visible check she can review. The problem is the structure of the work, not the model's ability.

questions.mindset: Separate creating from checking, and make the check produce something a human can see.

questions.stem: A marketing coordinator needs a product announcement in English, adapted for French and German markets. Legal must approve the English claims before anything is published. She asks for all three versions in one prompt, and each time legal edits the English, the other two versions no longer match. What is the BEST way to structure the work?

options.text: Keep generating all three versions in one prompt, but add an instruction that the translations must match the English exactly.
Finalize the English version and get legal approval first, then have Claude adapt the approved text for each market as a separate step.
Create the French and German versions first so that legal can review all three languages side by side in a single pass.
Ask Claude to produce the three versions at the same time in separate chats so that each version gets its full attention.

questions.explanation: The English text is the source the other two versions must match, and legal approval is a **gate**: nothing should be built on wording that is still changing. Sequencing the work as approve, then adapt, means each adaptation starts from final, approved wording, so edits stop breaking the match. This is chaining ordered by dependency: each step consumes the checked output of the step before it, instead of work being redone whenever an upstream input changes.

whyWrong.A: Any legal edit still requires redoing everything, and an "exact match" instruction cannot follow edits made after the versions were generated.
whyWrong.C: This reverses the dependency: the translations are produced before their source is final, so every legal edit makes them out of date.
whyWrong.D: Producing the versions in parallel only makes sense for independent pieces of work. These versions all depend on one approved source, so separate chats would still drift apart.

questions.mindset: Order steps by dependency: approve the source before building anything on it.

questions.scenario: An operations manager is producing a 30-page process manual with Claude, working from an approved outline and drafting one section at a time over several days. Each section is good on its own, but they use different names for the same team ("Fulfilment," "Dispatch," "Shipping Ops"), and two sections describe the same approval step differently.
questions.stem: Which TWO changes would MOST effectively fix this while keeping the section-by-section approach? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep a short sheet of agreed terms and process decisions, and supply it with the outline for every section.
Drop the section-by-section approach and generate the full manual in a single prompt so Claude sees everything at once.
Once all sections are drafted, run a separate consistency-review step that lists conflicting terms and process descriptions for her to resolve.
Add the line "be consistent with the earlier sections" to each new section prompt without changing anything else.
Ask Claude to write longer, more detailed sections so that each one fully explains its own terms and steps.

questions.explanation: When work is split by section, each step only sees what you give it. The fix has two parts. **Prevention:** give every section the same shared reference (agreed terms and decisions) along with the outline. Keeping it as Project knowledge makes it available in every chat (A). **Detection:** add a final consistency-review step that brings any remaining conflicts to her for a decision (C). This keeps the benefits of focused sections and removes the drift between them. Fixing output consistency with an explicit, fixed structure is a documented consistency technique.

whyWrong.B: A 30-page manual in one prompt loses the reviewable, fix-one-part benefits of working by section, and a single long output does not guarantee consistent terms.
whyWrong.D: "Be consistent" without supplying the earlier decisions asks Claude to match information it may not have, especially across separate days and chats.
whyWrong.E: Longer sections give each one more room to invent its own terms. The problem is a missing shared reference, not missing detail.

questions.mindset: When you split work into parts, give every part the same shared reference and add a final step that checks they fit together.

questions.stem: A procurement specialist must compare three vendors' service agreements, each about 25 pages, on renewal terms, liability caps, termination notice and data-handling commitments. Her single prompt, "Which contract is best for us?", returned an answer that gave one vendor's notice period to another vendor. What is the MOST effective way to restructure the task?

options.text: Ask the same question again, but tell Claude to be especially careful not to mix up details between the vendors.
Ask Claude to recommend the best contract first, then in a follow-up ask it to justify that choice with clause references.
Extract the same four terms from each contract into one table with clause references, check it, then compare.
Ask for a full summary of all three contracts in a single response so that she can read them side by side herself.

questions.explanation: Mixing up details between documents is a sign that one step is doing too much. Splitting **by item** (one contract at a time) and **by stage** (extract, check, then compare) fixes this. Using the same four fields for each contract keeps the extractions consistent. Working from the source text first, before drawing conclusions, is exactly the sequence Anthropic recommends for long documents; clause references let her verify each value quickly, and the comparison then rests on a table she has checked. For a binding contract decision, she would still involve legal or contract owners as her organization requires.

whyWrong.A: Asking for care adds emphasis without changing the structure, so the same overloaded single step can mix up details again.
whyWrong.B: Deciding first and justifying afterwards encourages Claude to find support for a choice that may rest on mixed-up facts. The facts need checking before the decision.
whyWrong.D: A long combined summary is the overloaded output that caused the mix-up, and it leaves her to do the structured comparison by hand.

questions.mindset: Extract the facts the same way for each item, verify them, and only then compare.

questions.scenario: An operations coordinator has used Claude to map out a weekly reporting job: pull figures from the CRM, the ticketing system and the finance system; reconcile them; calculate 12 KPIs; build a dashboard; and email it automatically to 40 managers every Monday. He wants the whole thing to run without anyone touching it.
questions.stem: Now that the job is broken into stages, what is the MOST appropriate next step for him in an Associate role?

options.text: Put every stage into one long prompt and set a weekly reminder to paste it into Claude each Monday morning.
Ask Claude to write the integration scripts, then deploy and schedule them himself on a shared team server.
Drop the idea, because jobs that span several business systems are not a good fit for Claude at all.
Give the stage breakdown to the developer or architect team as requirements, and keep using Claude in chat for the commentary.

questions.explanation: Breaking the job down did its work: it showed that the request is a **multi-system automated build** (integrations, scheduled runs, automatic distribution). The exam guide expects Associates to recognize limitations and hand complex or technical builds to Claude Developers and Architects. His breakdown makes a strong requirements document for that team. He can still use Claude in conversation for the parts that suit an Associate, such as analysing the figures and drafting the commentary.

whyWrong.A: A manual weekly paste is not the hands-off process he wants, and one giant prompt across five stages with several data sources removes the checkpoints that decomposition provides.
whyWrong.B: Deploying scripts that connect to the CRM and finance systems goes beyond the Associate role and skips engineering review, security and access controls.
whyWrong.C: Over-correction. The job is a good candidate for Claude-assisted automation. It just needs the right people to build it.

questions.mindset: Decomposition also shows you which parts are yours and which belong to a technical build team.

questions.stem: A department head asks a team assistant to "use Claude to make our onboarding better." The assistant isn't sure whether that means a new-hire checklist, a welcome guide, or a redesigned first-week schedule. What is the BEST first step?

options.text: Ask Claude to produce all three deliverables in full straight away so the department head can choose the one she prefers.
Have Claude list the open questions and assumptions, confirm them with the department head, then plan the steps.
Ask Claude for the single best way to improve onboarding and then carry out whatever it recommends in that answer.
Ask Claude to draft a detailed welcome guide, since that is the most common onboarding document in most organizations.

questions.explanation: The first part of a vague, complex request is **defining it**. Using Claude to bring out the open questions and hidden assumptions (goal, audience, format, constraints) and confirming them with the person who asked means the later steps work toward the right target. It is the cheapest checkpoint in the whole chain: a few minutes now prevents a polished deliverable nobody asked for.

whyWrong.A: Building three complete deliverables to avoid one clarifying conversation wastes effort, and none of them may match what she actually meant.
whyWrong.C: Claude's "best way" is a guess without the department head's goals and constraints. It skips the scoping decision only she can make.
whyWrong.D: Picking the most common deliverable is guessing at the goal. If it's wrong, all the drafting work is wasted.

questions.mindset: With an ambiguous request, the first step is to define it, and the person who asked confirms that definition.

questions.scenario: A policy analyst must brief her director on a 280-page government consultation report with 14 chapters. She pasted the whole report and asked for "a two-page summary." The result covered the early chapters well but barely mentioned the later ones, including the chapter that matters most to her organization.
questions.stem: Which TWO actions would MOST effectively improve the summary? Choose TWO.

options.text: Ask Claude to confirm that it has read every page of the report before it writes the two-page summary.
Summarize one chapter at a time using the same short template, checking each chapter summary as she goes.
Ask for a much longer, ten-page summary so that the later chapters have enough room to be included.
Write the two-page brief from the checked chapter summaries, telling Claude which chapter matters most so it gets priority.
Regenerate the two-page summary several times and merge the strongest parts of each version into one brief.

questions.explanation: Squeezing a very long document into one summary in a single step leads to uneven coverage. Splitting **by section** (B) makes every chapter get the same focused treatment, and the shared template makes the summaries comparable and quick to check. The **synthesis step** (D) then builds the brief from verified pieces, with her priorities stated explicitly instead of left for Claude to guess. Together they form a map-then-combine chain with a human check in the middle.

whyWrong.A: A model saying it has read everything is not evidence of balanced coverage, and the request is still one overloaded step.
whyWrong.C: A longer summary changes the length, not the method, and the director needs two pages. Coverage can still be uneven, just with more words.
whyWrong.E: Regenerating without changing the structure gives more versions of the same imbalance, and merging them by hand adds work with no check against the source.

questions.mindset: For very long material, summarize each part with the same template, check the parts, then combine them with clear priorities.
